food.text: After the Jōmon period (14,000–300 BCE), Japanese society shifted from a semi-sedentary hunter-gatherer lifestyle to an agricultural one. Rice cultivation began around the third century BCE, having been introduced from China.
The Yayoi period arrived in Japan with immigrants from mainland East Asia. They introduced rice agriculture and other elements of continental material culture to the Japanese archipelago.
The Three Kingdoms period (57 BCE – 668 CE) was one of rapid cultural evolution in Korea. Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla each had their own distinct set of cultural practices and foods.

Rice farming is believed to have reached Japan by a long route. It went from the Yangtze River Delta to the Shandong peninsula, then to the Liaodong peninsula, and finally to the Korean peninsula. From there it was introduced directly to the Japanese archipelago.
Among Korea's Three Kingdoms, Baekje lay in the southwestern part of the peninsula. It was known for cold foods and for fermented foods like kimchi.

Dotori-muk, or acorn jelly, originated in ancient times in Korea. Oak trees in mountains across the country produced acorns each autumn in quantities abundant enough to be a viable source of food. The jelly does not spoil easily, which suited it to long travels. During the first of the Japanese invasions of Joseon, King Seonjo took refuge in the north, and food shortages caused by the invasion made it difficult for villagers to find anything to serve the king and his entourage, so they hurriedly made them dotori-muk.

Once rice arrived in Japan, it was commonly boiled plain and called gohan or meshi. Both words came to mean "meal" as well. Peasants often mixed millet with rice, especially in mountainous regions where rice did not proliferate.

During Japan's Kofun period (300 to 538 CE), Chinese culture was introduced into Japan from Korea. A cow or horse would be ritually sacrificed on the first day of rice paddy cultivation, a ritual introduced from China. Such animals were otherwise rare and more valued for providing labor and transportation.

art.text: The earliest Japanese architecture consisted of simple pit-houses and stores adapted to the needs of a hunter-gatherer population. Later, influence from Han dynasty China via Korea brought more complex grain stores and ceremonial burial chambers.

The origins of painting in Japan reach back into its prehistoric period. Simple stick figures and geometric designs appear on Jōmon period pottery and on dōtaku bronze bells of the Yayoi period, which lasted from 300 BC to 300 AD.

Bronze production in Korea began in the Middle Mumun period and became increasingly important in ceremonial and political society after 700 BC. Bronze daggers, mirrors, jewelry and weaponry have been found, along with evidence of walled-town polities.

Mural paintings with both geometric and figurative designs have been found in numerous tumulus from the Kofun period, which ran from 300 to 700 AD. These painted burial mounds are among the earliest surviving Japanese murals.

Raised-floor architecture first appeared on the Korean peninsula in the Middle Mumun, around 850 to 550 BC. Before that, Mumun period buildings were pit dwellings with walls of wattle-and-daub and thatched roofs.

Buddhist icons reached Japan through immigrant groups after Northern Wei Buddhist art had spread into the Korean peninsula. The Three Kingdoms, and particularly Baekje, were active agents in introducing Buddhism to Japan in 538 or 552.

The introduction of Buddhism in Japan during the sixth century was a catalyst for large-scale temple building using complicated techniques in wood. This marked a shift from the simple structures of earlier times.
Important elements of the architectural style of Baekje were later adopted by Japan. Baekje had assimilated diverse influences and expressed its derivation from Chinese models.

Korean music reached the Japanese imperial court first, possibly as early as the third century. It was at first called sankangaku, covering all the Korean states, and later komagaku, referring to the court music of Goguryeo.

war.text: Near the end of the Jōmon period (c. 1000 BC), villages and towns in Japan were surrounded by moats and wooden fences because of growing violence within and between communities. Battles were fought with swords, slings, spears, and bows and arrows. Some human remains have been found with arrow wounds.

In 108 BC, the Chinese Han dynasty defeated Wiman Joseon and installed four commanderies in the northern Korean peninsula. Three of them fell or retreated westward within a few decades. The defeat marked the end of Gojoseon in the late 2nd century BC.

The Three Kingdoms of Korea often warred with each other, and Silla was frequently dominated by Baekje and Goguryeo. By the 2nd century Silla was a large state in the southeast, occupying and influencing its neighbouring city-states. Though the smallest and weakest of the three, it used cunning diplomacy to make opportunistic pacts with stronger Korean kingdoms.

The recorded military history of Japan began in the 2nd century, during the Yayoi period. In the 5th century, the Yamato tribal alliance fought among the Three Kingdoms of Korea, taking on Goguryeo and Silla.

The Yayoi arrived in Japan endowed with bronze and iron weapons and tools, initially imported from China and the Korean peninsula. They radiated out from northern Kyūshū and gradually supplanted the Jōmon. Radio-carbon evidence now suggests this phase began between 1,000 and 800 BC, some 500 years earlier than once thought.

In southern Korea, the Mumun era was the first in which chiefdoms rose, expanded, and collapsed. An increase in local conflicts, along with long-distance trade and the introduction of bronze and iron metallurgy, marked the end of the Mumun around 300 BC.

The Lelang Commandery, set up by the Han dynasty after its conquest in 108 BC, survived as a center of cultural and economic exchange with successive Chinese dynasties for four centuries. It ended in 313 AD, when it was conquered by Goguryeo.

After Gojoseon fell, the state of Buyeo arose in today's North Korea and southern Manchuria and lasted from about the 2nd century BC to 494 AD. Goguryeo absorbed its remnants in 494. Both Goguryeo and Baekje considered themselves its successor.

literature.text: Before kanji arrived from China, Japan had no writing system. It is believed that Chinese characters came to Japan at the very beginning of the 5th century, brought by immigrants from Korea and China.

In ancient Korea, songs were part of religious life, and Chinese dynastic histories vividly record their performance. At state assemblies the chief ritualist told the story of the founder's divine origin and his deeds in war and peace. He mixed the story with primal songs that welcomed, entertained and sent off gods and spirits.
A famous surviving example of early Korean poetry dates to 17 BC. It is Yuri's Song of the Yellow Bird (Hwangjoga), written to lament the departure of his Chinese concubine Chihui.
One famous early lyric song is the Gonghuin (Konghu-in) by Yeo-ok, from the time of Gojoseon. It is counted among the earliest songs of Korean literature.
The first poem documented in both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki is attributed to a kami named Susanoo. He made a poem (an uta, or waka) when he married Princess Kushinada in Izumo Province.

Sijo, Korea's favorite poetic genre, flowered greatest in the 16th and 17th centuries under the Joseon dynasty. Yet the earliest surviving poem of the genre comes from the 4th century, and its roots lie in earlier forms.

Many of the poetic pieces recorded in the Kojiki were perhaps transmitted from the time the Japanese had no writing. Hieda no Are recited the mythology and history, and Ō no Yasumaro recorded it in 712. The Nihon Shoki also contains many poetic pieces.

science.text: Around the 3rd century BC, the Yayoi people arrived in the Japanese archipelago and introduced iron technology and agricultural civilization. Because they farmed, the Yayoi population grew rapidly and ultimately overwhelmed the hunter-gatherer Jōmon people.

Farmers of the Mumun Period in Korea began using multiple cropping systems some time after 1500 BC. This advance in food production hastened the beginnings of intensive agriculture on the peninsula, and paddy-field wet-rice cultivation was also introduced into the south.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: The Yayoi brought more than farming to Japan. They also introduced weaving and silk production, new woodworking methods, glassmaking technology, and new architectural styles. They radiated out from northern Kyūshū, gradually supplanting the Jōmon.
Korea and adjacent areas of East Asia seem to have been part of the domestication region of soybean between 1500 and 500 BC. Paddy-field rice was also cultivated in Bronze Age Korea.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Korean iron production was adopted several hundred years after bronze, and Korean-made iron tools and weapons became increasingly common after about 200 BC. Iron tools helped intensive agriculture spread into new areas of the Korean Peninsula.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Gayan immigrants founded Japan's first iron production and its sue pottery style. Mass migrations of Gayans to Japan, often to escape strife with neighboring Korean states, let Japan make some products it had previously needed to import.
science.source_title: Relations between Gaya and ancient Japan

science.text: Radio-carbon evidence now suggests that the Yayoi wave of technological change began between 1,000 and 800 BC. That is some 500 years earlier than the date of around 400 BC that was long accepted.

Moulds for bronze casting found at Songguk-ri show that people in southern Korea were producing bronze themselves from about 700 BC. Before 900 BC, bronze objects had only been traded in from outside the peninsula.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Industrial-scale production of pottery and roof tiles became notable in Korea after the adoption of Chinese dragon kiln, or climbing kiln, technology. This happened sometime between AD 100 and 300.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Around 300 BC, agriculture and metallurgy from the regions of Korea that later became Gaya were introduced into Japan. This helped bring the transition from hunter-gatherer Jōmon culture to Yayoi culture. Historians remain unsure whether this came through invasion or through native adoption of imports.
science.source_title: Relations between Gaya and ancient Japan

science.text: After 850 BC, archaeological evidence shows the way Koreans heated their homes changed. Hearths dug into pit-house floors disappeared and were likely replaced by some kind of brazier-like technology in Hoseo, Honam and western Yeongnam.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Under-floor heating, called ondol, was long thought to be a Korean invention, first made by the people of the Northern Okjeo around 2,500 years ago. Then a roughly 3,000-year-old equivalent system was found in Alaska. One hypothesis says whale-hunting people from the Korean peninsula may have migrated there by sea.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

politics.text: The kingdom of Gojoseon, which tradition says was founded in 2333 BC, fell to the Han dynasty in 108 BC. It was followed by the Three Kingdoms period, in which Korea was divided into Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla.

By the end of the 4th century, the Yamato clan was well established on the Nara plain, with considerable control over the surrounding areas. The Five kings of Wa sent envoys to China to have their dominion of the Japanese Islands recognized.
The name Korea comes from Goryeo, which was first used by Goguryeo in the early 5th century. Goryeo was founded in 918 as Goguryeo's successor and inherited its name.

Chinese sources such as the Shangshu dazhuan and the Book of Documents claim that in the 12th century BCE a Shang dynasty sage named Jizi, also called Kija, immigrated to the region. The Samguk Yusa adds that King Wu of Zhou placed him on the throne of Old Chosŏn in 1122 BCE, succeeding Tan'gun.

Old Chosŏn appears in the records of Guanzi trading with the state of Qi. The Shiji began referring to it as a country from 195 BCE onwards, though Mark E. Byington says it is entirely unclear whether it was a state-level polity.

Around 300 BC, a state called Jin arose in the southern Korean peninsula. Very little is known about it, but it established relations with Han China and exported artifacts to the Yayoi of Japan. Around 100 BC, Jin evolved into the Samhan confederacies.
Goguryeo was founded in 37 BC by Jumong, who was posthumously given the royal title Dongmyeongseong. Later, King Taejo centralized the government.

Baekje was founded around modern-day Seoul by a Goguryeo prince, a son of the founder of Goguryeo. It absorbed all of the Mahan states and subjugated most of the western Korean peninsula, including the modern provinces of Gyeonggi, Chungcheong, and Jeolla, to a centralised government.

Some Korean scholars hold that Old Chosŏn's center only moved to Pyongyang after the Yan conquest of Liaodong in 300 BCE. Its earlier location has been debated since the Joseon period and was highly controversial in the 20th century.
Goguryeo was the first Korean kingdom to adopt Buddhism as the state religion. This happened in 372, during the reign of King Sosurim.

Baekje was once a great military power, most notably in the 4th century under Geunchogo. Its influence extended across the sea to Liaoxi and Shandong in China and to Kyushu in Japan, but Gwanggaeto the Great critically defeated it and it declined.

The Nihon Shoki states that the Yamato were strong enough to send an army against the powerful northern Korean state of Goguryeo. Yamato Japan also had close relations with the southwestern Korean kingdom of Baekje.

In the Middle Mumun period (850 to 550 BC), the first societies led by big-men or chiefs emerged in southern Korea. Bronze production began then and grew increasingly important in ceremonial and political society after 700 BC.

philosophy.text: Korean shamanism is described as the oldest indigenous religion of Korea. It has been passed down from prehistory to the present and dates back as far as Old Joseon. Its ritual specialists, called mudang, are typically women.

Kami veneration, the heart of what became Shinto, has been traced back to Japan's Yayoi period (300 BCE to 250 CE). Kami are believed to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent landscape locations.
Buddhism was introduced to Korea from China during the Three Kingdoms era, in the fourth century. It went on to become an important part of Korean culture for many centuries.

In Korean shamanism, the mudang act as mediators between humans and the supernatural world. In gut rituals they offer food and drink to gods and spirits, or entertain them with storytelling, song and dance.

Shinto places a major conceptual focus on ensuring purity, largely through cleaning practices such as ritual washing and bathing, especially before worship. The things it treats as particular pollutants include death, disease, witchcraft, the flaying alive of an animal, incest, bestiality, excrement, and blood from menstruation or childbirth. Purification restores harmony between humans and the kami, and animal sacrifice is not an appropriate offering because the shedding of blood is seen as a polluting act.

Anthropological studies link the Korean ancestral god Dangun to Tengri, meaning "Heaven", the shaman and the prince. The Korean mudang is also compared to the Japanese miko, and Korean Muism has similarities with Japanese Shinto.

Korean shamanism has no central authority, and belief and practice vary widely. The largest type of mudang, the mansin, are personally possessed by deities or ancestral spirits, while the sesŭp-mu of eastern and southern regions act as spirit mediums without possession.

culture.text: Jōmon pottery is noted for its decoration, made by pressing cords into the wet outside of the clay. The Jōmon people were hunter-gatherers and early agriculturalists who reached a considerable degree of sedentism and cultural complexity.

Around 400 BCE, a mass migration crossed the Korean Strait from the Korean Peninsula to Kyushu and the Chūgoku region of Honshu. It led to conflicts between the indigenous Jōmon people and the immigrant Yayoi people, and it was partly driven by the violent wars and regional chaos of the late Eastern Zhou dynasty. The Yayoi brought pottery, bronze, iron and better metalworking, which improved farming tools and weaponry, while the Jōmon hunter-gatherer lifestyle declined and wet-rice farming rose.

Around 250 CE, the Kofun period began, and Japan's elites built gigantic tombs called kofun. They point to powerful warrior elites, fueled by more intensive agriculture and the introduction of iron technologies.
The oldest indigenous religion of Korea is Korean folk religion, or Korean shamanism. It has been passed down from prehistory to the present, long before Buddhism arrived from China.
Jōmon people made tools and jewelry from bone, stone, shell and antler. They also made pottery figurines and vessels, and lacquerware.

Contact with the Korean Peninsula slowly increased during the Final Jōmon period. Korean-type settlements appeared in western Kyushu from around 900 BCE, and the settlers brought wet rice farming, bronze and iron metallurgy, and pottery styles like those of the Mumun period. They coexisted with Jōmon and Yayoi settlements for around a thousand years.
Buddhism entered Korea from China during the Three Kingdoms period, in 372, which is in the 4th century. It later became the dominant religious and cultural influence in the Silla and Goryeo states.

Japan's traditional founding date, set by Emperor Jimmu, is February 11, 660 BCE. That story comes from the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, Japan's first written records, which date from the 6th to 8th centuries. Even so, it shows little relation to what archaeologists now understand of Jōmon culture.

Bear worship was an important element of the Okhotsk culture, which originated in the 5th century from the Susuya culture of southern Sakhalin and northwestern Hokkaido. It was uncommon in the Jōmon period of Japan. The practice was shared by various Northern Eurasian peoples, including the Ainu and the Nivkh.

From the mid-fifth century, people from Baekje and Gaya, known as Toraijin, immigrated to Japan. Many were refugees who came during the intense regional warfare that racked the Korean peninsula between the late fourth and late seventh centuries. They brought knowledge of iron metallurgy, stoneware pottery, law and Chinese writing.
Yayoi-styled pottery has been found in a Jōmon site in northern Kyushu dating to 800 BCE. That is earlier than the Yayoi period's start, placed between 500 and 300 BCE by radio-carbon evidence.
